content: 1. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) coverage has been introduced in selected priority populations to reduce the risk of HIV transmission. This intervention targets groups at higher risk of acquiring HIV. 2. Universal precautions in healthcare settings include ensuring injection safety and the proper disposal of injection equipment. These measures are critical to preventing nosocomial transmission of bloodborne pathogens such as HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis. 3. A tool has been developed and successfully used to conduct national surveys on injection safety. This tool assesses the safety of procedures such as phlebotomy, lancet use, intravenous injections, and infusions. 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides guidance on indicators for monitoring and reporting the health sector's response to HIV/AIDS. This includes facility-level injection safety, which measures the percentage of healthcare facilities using new, disposable, single-use injection equipment for all therapeutic injections. 5. The availability of needles and syringes is monitored by assessing the percentage of facilities reporting no stock-outs of new, single-use needles and syringes in the past 12 months. This reflects the program's ability to maintain necessary supplies for injection safety. 6. Blood transfusion safety is guided by a conceptual framework with five key components: establishing well-organized, nationally coordinated blood transfusion services; collecting blood from unpaid, low-risk volunteer donors; ensuring quality-assured testing for transfusion-transmissible infections; promoting the safe and appropriate use of blood; and implementing quality assurance systems throughout the transfusion process. 7. WHO recommends that all blood donations be screened for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis before use. However, in 2011, nearly one-quarter of blood donations in low-income countries were not screened according to basic quality procedures. 8. Facility-level blood safety is assessed by the percentage of healthcare facilities providing blood transfusions that meet requirements for sufficient and safe blood supply. This evaluates the effectiveness of policies and programs to ensure adequate and safe blood availability. 9. Globally, in 2012, there were an estimated 362 million new cases of curable sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis. Untreated STIs can lead to complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, stillbirths, neonatal death, and increased risk of HIV transmission. 10. Effective STI control depends on reliable and routine surveillance. Core components of STI surveillance include case reporting, prevalence assessments, monitoring the etiology of STI syndromes, and tracking antimicrobial resistance. 11. STI surveillance is a critical component of second-generation HIV surveillance systems. Monitoring incident STIs, such as urethral discharge in men or primary and secondary syphilis, can serve as an early warning of HIV epidemic potential and ongoing high-risk sexual activity. 12. Updated WHO guidelines for STI surveillance were released in 2012, reflecting advancements in diagnostic technologies and changes in epidemiology, such as the spread of antimicrobial-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae. 13. Strengthening STI case reporting can be based on syndromic or etiologic approaches, depending on the available resources. Syndromic reporting is common in settings with limited laboratory capacity, while etiologic surveillance is recommended in countries with sufficient diagnostic capabilities. 14. Periodic prevalence assessments, conducted every three to five years in selected population groups, provide national estimates of STI prevalence, identify high-risk groups, guide resource allocation, and monitor prevention program effectiveness. 15. Etiologic studies of STI syndromes are essential for updating treatment recommendations. These studies should be conducted every two to three years in different populations and geographic locations to assess the causative microorganisms of common STI syndromes. 16. Routine monitoring of antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae is critical due to the emergence of resistance to all known classes of antibiotics used for gonorrhea treatment. WHO recommends modifying national treatment guidelines when resistance levels reach 5% or higher. 17. STIs in pregnant women are of significant public health importance due to their potential to cause stillbirth, prematurity, low birth weight, neonatal death, and congenital infections. Surveillance and monitoring of syphilis in pregnancy are particularly important to eliminate mother-to-child transmission. 18. Syphilis screening coverage among antenatal care (ANC) attendees measures the extent of routine syphilis testing during pregnancy. Treatment of syphilis-seropositive pregnant women is necessary to prevent congenital syphilis. 19. Syphilis seroprevalence among key populations, such as sex workers and men who have sex with men, is a core indicator for guiding national STI responses. Data on these populations can be obtained through routine health information systems, sentinel surveillance, or special surveys. 20. Trends in syphilis seroprevalence should be interpreted cautiously unless consistent methods and populations are used across survey rounds.
